title: Neural networks as decision trees: an analytical solution for learning and neural selectivity
authors: Hugo Tissot, Jonas Ranft, Yves Boubenec
abstract: Nonlinear neural networks develop structured internal representations, yet how their geometry is determined by the tasks being learned remains poorly understood. Here, we develop an analytical framework for piecewise-linear feedforward and recurrent networks that links learning, activation-region structure, and neural selectivity. We show that, at any stationary point of gradient-aligned learning, a nonlinear network decomposes into local linear regressions over its activation regions. Deviations from the corresponding least-squares solutions are jointly constrained by network weights shared across regions and vanish in the low-error regime, yielding an approximate piecewise least-squares decomposition of the task. This structure admits a decision-tree interpretation, which we recover numerically by fitting trees to predict network activation patterns from the input. We further derive how the regions in which neurons are active determine the task statistics they capture, thereby organizing neural selectivity into distinct subpopulations. The resulting predictions closely match the selectivity geometry observed in simulated networks and two empirical neural datasets. Finally, we show that neural baseline regulates activation pattern diversity, placing networks along a continuum between coarse, generalizing representations and fine-grained, expressive representations. Together, these results establish activation regions as a unifying framework for describing how nonlinear networks decompose task structure into local computations and how those computations can be revealed through neural activity.
summary: This paper provides an analytical framework showing that nonlinear neural networks effectively decompose the task they learn into a set of local, piecewise linear regressions defined over distinct activation regions. This structure is mathematically equivalent to a decision tree, suggesting that network selectivity is organized modularly based on these regions. The work establishes activation regions as a unifying concept for understanding network computation.
main_problem: The paper aims to understand how the geometry of internal representations in nonlinear neural networks is determined by the specific tasks they are learning.
main_result: The network's computation decomposes into a piecewise least-squares structure across distinct activation regions, which can be interpreted as a decision tree.
method: An analytical framework is developed for gradient-aligned learning in piecewise-linear networks, deriving stationarity conditions based on regional gradient contributions.
model_or_system: The model analyzed is a piecewise-linear feedforward and recurrent neural network, whose activity is partitioned into 'activation regions' ($S_r$) defined by the fixed pattern of active/inactive hidden units.
key_observables: Activation regions ($S_r$), regional deviation ($\Delta_r$), selectivity geometry ($\Sigma$), and the resulting decision-tree structure.
important_parameters: The per-region training loss ($\ell_r$) and the network's baseline activity level, which regulates representation diversity.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a stationary point in gradient-aligned learning and that the regional input data ($X_r$) has full row rank for the least-squares decomposition.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the decomposition into a tree structure (Fig. 2) and show that the network's implemented map converges toward the local least-squares solution as training error decreases (Fig. 3).
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by establishing the analytical framework for gradient decomposition, showing the resulting piecewise least-squares approximation, interpreting this structure as a decision tree, and finally validating the prediction of selectivity geometry using task statistics.
why_interesting: The explicit mathematical link between optimization principles (least-squares) and the structural organization (decision trees) of high-dimensional representations is relevant for understanding how complex physical systems, including quantum information processing, might naturally organize their computational subspaces.
